title: this summers wildfires show why europeans must pay heed planetary boundaries  ecmii 2026 09 02
author: Luc Bas
text:
September 1 - Few summers in recent memory have tested Europe the way this one has. Wildfires have burned through 116,000 hectares in Spain, 79,000 in Italy, 47,000 in Portugal, 42,000 in France and close to 24,000 in Greece. Europe's major rivers, the Seine, the Rhine, and the ​Danube, have fallen to record lows, and nearly 10,000 excess deaths across five countries have already been linked to ‌extreme heat.
Belgium, my home, has not been spared, issuing its own national heatwave alert in June, when temperatures were forecast to reach 38 degrees Celsius, and the recent immense wildfire in Wallonia, which destroyed 3,000 hectares of dried out bogs.
These are not separate crises. They are connected symptoms of mounting pressure on the planetary boundaries, ​the Earth system limits that keep our food, water and economies stable. This summer demonstrates what that pressure looks like when ​it hits an entire continent at once, and it is this reality that I now face as Belgium’s ⁠recently appointed chief planetary officer (CPO).
The idea behind this new role is to ensure that climate change risk assessments reach the people who set ​budgets, plan infrastructure and decide how we prepare the country for what is coming. It ensures that planetary boundaries science, which helps us ​understand the interconnected pressures behind crises like these, isn’t just a concept that scientists discuss amongst themselves.
Belgium had a climate wake-up call in July 2021, when unprecedented rainfall caused the most devastating floods in our modern history. The floods killed 39 people, displaced 16,000, and cost an estimated 5.2 billion euros.
Out of that experience came ​CERAC, Belgium’s Climate Risk Assessment Center, of which I am director. CERAC reports directly to our National Security Council. Part of CERAC’s job ​is to translate planetary boundaries science into measurable risks.
The risks CERAC is identifying are not theoretical. A CERAC study found that we are already exceeding our ‌fair share ⁠of the global carbon budget. It linked air pollution to roughly 2,940 premature deaths in Belgium in 2023. Another projected more than 1,000 additional heat-related deaths a year once warming reaches 2C. That study was published long before this summer's headlines caught up.
When appointing me as CPO in June, Jean-Luc Crucke, Belgium's Minister of Mobility and Climate, said that by creating the role, Belgium is using the best available science on ​planetary boundaries to inform policy and ​investment decisions, including linking it ⁠to national security strategy, because in a world of increasingly systemic risk, doing so is no longer optional. That sums up the whole argument in a single sentence.
Belgium is not alone in struggling to coordinate climate ​and environmental risk across different levels of government. Similar fragmentation exists around the world. This appointment is ​one of the ⁠most direct attempts yet to address this, but it is not an isolated one.
Planetary guardians, together with Earth system scientist Johan Rockstrom, are building a worldwide network of CPOs. More countries are expected to name their chief planetary scientists or officers by the end of the year, each tailored to ⁠their institutions ​rather than modeled directly on Belgium's.
Watching this summer’s fires and droughts spread across Europe, ​I realised that without mechanisms to translate planetary risk directly into decision-making, policymakers risk failing to protect their citizens from the threats that are bearing down on them.
I hope ​more governments across Europe and beyond reach the same conclusion soon, rather than waiting for a disaster of their own to force the decision.
